skip_reason: Inbound service-recovery call on a move that has already been executed, not a new-business sales conversation. Missy Howard opens with "Couple of your guys have been here moving. They left quite a bit of stuff and just said that they couldn't fit it in their truck" — the crew has already loaded, left and is driving to Katy overnight. The entire call is about recovering the items left behind on a completed job: Jules checks for options, explains trucks are not shared between customers, floats sending a second crew and truck the next day, and ends by committing his branch manager to a callback. There is no lead intake, no quote form, no pricing, no estimate and no booking attempt — the job was sold and performed before the call began. The 85-point sales scorecard does not apply and this call should not count toward the sales grading average.
top_strength: Jules absorbed a genuinely angry customer without getting defensive and moved her toward a next step. Missy came in hot — "we're kind of shut out of luck right now and I'm kinda pissed off" — and Jules led with ownership rather than explanation: "I'm so sorry about that. I get it." He repeated that acknowledgment each time she escalated ("For sure I understand. I'm so sorry about that"), and he never argued with her account of what the crew was told. He was also honest about the limits of his own authority instead of bluffing — "unfortunately, I think my branch manager already left for today. So I'm not quite sure how to go about this right now" — while still putting a concrete, plausible remedy on the table: "what we can do is tomorrow we can send two guys in another truck to pick up the rest of the items." He gave a real reason for declining her consolidation idea rather than a flat no ("we do not share your trucks with other customers because sometimes things get lost"), asked the one operationally useful question in the call — whether she had "wiggle room for the move out" — and closed with a specific, ownable commitment: "I will have my branch manager give you a callback first thing in the morning, would that be okay?" She ended the call at "Okay, I appreciate it thank you," which is a real recovery from where it started.
coaching_note: Not scored on the sales rubric — this is a claims/service-recovery call. The coaching observation worth passing along: Jules made a promise on someone else's behalf and left no trace to guarantee it. He committed his branch manager to a callback "first thing in the morning" on a Friday night, but never confirmed Missy's callback number, never restated her destination timing back to her, and answered her one identity check with only "Yup! I have it here." Nothing in the call indicates a note was written on the job. The customer is now driving to Katy with her belongings split across two cities, her stated fallback is eighty-year-old parents making a four-and-a-half hour drive, and the entire resolution depends on a manager walking in Monday and independently knowing to call. The fix is to close service-recovery calls the way a booking closes: read the callback number back, capture what was left behind and where, log it on the job, and tell the customer what was written down. He also surfaced a useful detail — she had "a little bit of movement wiggle room" on the move-out — and then let it go without pinning down how much, which is exactly the constraint the manager will need first thing. Worth flagging separately to Amanda as a claims-adjacent escalation, since it involves a crew leaving contracted items behind on a long-haul move.
phone_presence_notes: Warm and steady under real customer anger — Jules repeatedly named the frustration instead of deflecting ("I'm so sorry about that. I get it," "I completely understand") and never got defensive about the crew, and the customer's tone moved from "I'm kinda pissed off" to "Okay, I appreciate it thank you," though several long "Let me see" stalls left dead air where a status narration would have held her better.
